STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

A classification tree repeatedly divides the feature space into regions. Each terminal leaf predicts a class or class probability.

Every problem starts with data. We have measurements for fruit — Weight (x-axis) and Color Intensity (y-axis).

Each fruit is already labeled: an Apple or an Orange. The goal of our tree is to learn rules to sort them into cleaner groups.

The Whole Idea of Classification Trees

A Classification Tree is a supervised machine-learning model that learns a sequence of simple yes/no flowchart-like questions to sort data into categories.

Raw Labeled Data → Root Node → Scan Best Question → Split Data → Repeat Recursively → Leaf Prediction → Evaluation
Tiny Tree Dictionary
• Feature: A measurable property or input variable used to make predictions (e.g., Weight, Color Intensity).
• Label: The target outcome or true answer we want the model to predict (e.g., Apple, Orange).
• Class: One of the specific categorical outcomes (e.g., Apples vs. Oranges).
• Root Node: The very first top-level block containing 100% of the training data.
• Split: A division of a parent node into two child nodes based on a feature question.
• Child Node: The subgroups created after splitting a parent node.
• Leaf Node: A final terminal node that does not split further. It makes the final prediction.
• Impurity: A measure of how mixed or diverse the class labels are within a particular node.
• Gini Impurity: A mathematical metric used to calculate impurity (0.0 means perfectly pure; 0.5 is the maximum for a balanced binary node).
• Weighted Impurity: The combined impurity of child nodes, weighted by the proportion of samples that went into each child.
• Impurity Decrease: The difference between parent Gini and weighted child Gini. The tree maximizes this "gain".
• Decision Boundary: The geometric line(s) dividing different class zones on the coordinate map.
• Tree Depth: The length of the longest path from the root node down to any leaf node.
• Pruning: Cutting back branches to simplify the model and improve generalizability on unseen data.
• Overfitting: Memorizing noise in the training set, causing failure on unseen test data.
• Underfitting: Creating a model that is too simple (e.g. too shallow) to learn the real underlying patterns.

STAGE 02 · PREPARE
The Train / Test Split

To build a robust model, we never evaluate our tree on the exact same data it used for learning. Instead, we divide our original dataset into two parts:

Data Partitioning
Training Set

Used to scan thresholds, calculate Gini, and build rules.
Count: 28 fruits

Test Set (Held out)

Count: 6 fruits

⚠️ Data Leakage Warning: Using test data to choose splits, tune tree depth, or pick stopping criteria is a cardinal sin of machine learning. The test set must ONLY be used for final generalizability assessment.

CHECK YOUR KNOWLEDGE

Why is a Train/Test split essential for decision trees?

It helps the tree grow deeper and generate more rules.
It allows us to detect overfitting by measuring performance on unseen samples.
It guarantees that Gini impurity reaches exactly 0.0.
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
The Root Node

At the very beginning, a Classification Tree puts all the training data into one big group on the fruit map. We call this the Root Node.

This starting box is very "messy" because it contains a mix of both apples and oranges. The tree's job is to split this box into smaller, cleaner sub-groups.

STAGE 04 · UNDERSTAND
Measuring Messiness

To split effectively, the tree needs a way to measure how mixed a box is. We use a math rule called Gini Impurity.

A Gini score of 0.0 means the box is perfectly pure. For this binary example, 0.5 is the maximum at a 50/50 mix; multiclass maxima differ.

Gini Impurity Formula

Gini = 1 - Σ pᵢ²

For two classes (Apple & Orange):
Gini = 1 - [ P(Apple)² + P(Orange)² ]
    
Live Root Node Calculation
• Total training fruit (N): 28
• Apples (🍎): 14
• Oranges (🍊): 14

P(Apple) = 14 / 28 = 0.50
P(Orange) = 14 / 28 = 0.50

Gini = 1 - [ P(Apple)² + P(Orange)² ]
Gini = 1 - [ (0.50)² + (0.50)² ]
Gini = 1 - [ 0.25 + 0.25 ] = 0.50

💡 Meaning: This root node is very mixed because it contains equal numbers of Apples and Oranges.
Gini Impurity vs. Entropy

While Gini is highly popular in CART (Classification and Regression Trees), another metric called Entropy is also widely used:

Entropy = - Σ pᵢ log₂(pᵢ)

Both metrics measure the same core property: disorder. A node with equal proportions of classes has a Gini score of 0.50 and an Entropy score of 1.0. Both reach 0.0 when a node is perfectly pure. In practice, Gini and entropy often choose very similar splits, but not always. This guide uses Gini because it is simple, common, and easy to compute.

CONCEPT QUIZ

What does a Gini Impurity of 0.0 indicate about a subset of fruit?

The subset contains exactly 50% Apples and 50% Oranges.
The subset is 100% pure (contains only one type of fruit).
The subset is empty.
STAGE 05 · OBSERVE
Testing Every Question

How does the tree find the best split? It tries testing candidate split points between observed values across the map.

Because the tree asks one feature question at a time (e.g., "Is Weight < X?"), each possible split becomes a straight vertical or horizontal cut across the graph. Watch the sweeping line on the canvas analyze both features.

The Candidate Search Strategy

How does a decision tree find the best threshold? It doesn't guess random decimals. Instead, it uses a deterministic mathematical process:

Sort values: For a given feature (like Weight), it sorts all observed training values in ascending order.
Compute Midpoints: It calculates the halfway points (midpoints) between every adjacent pair of unique values.
Evaluate Splits: It treats each midpoint as a candidate threshold (e.g., Weight < 5.40), splits the data, and evaluates the resulting weighted Gini impurity.

STAGE 06 · BUILD
How the Tree Scores One Split

The tree found the single best question! By splitting the data at this specific threshold, it gets the lowest possible combined Gini impurity.

This first split is often very influential because it shapes the rest of the tree. It divides the fruit map cleanly into two distinct regions.

The Golden Question
Best Split: Color < 5.50
How the Tree Scores This Split
🥇 Chosen Split Question: Color < 5.50

• Total Samples: 13
• Apples (🍎): 0 | Oranges (🍊): 13

Right Child (No):

Weighted Gini = (N_left / N) × Gini_left + (N_right / N) × Gini_right
Weighted Gini = (13/28 × 0.000) + (15/28 × 0.124) ≈ 0.067

Gini Decrease = Root Gini - Weighted Gini = 0.500 - 0.067 = 0.433
SPLIT CALCULATION QUIZ

What property makes a candidate split the absolute "winner" in a decision tree?

It always splits the dataset exactly 50/50 by quantity.
It yields the largest Gini impurity decrease (lowest weighted children impurity).
It guarantees that both left and right child nodes become 100% pure instantly.
STAGE 07 · BUILD
Recursive Splitting

The tree isn't done. It now treats each of the two new boxes as a separate problem, and asks again: "Can I perform another split to make these even cleaner?"

It repeats this process recursively, carving the map into smaller and smaller axis-aligned rectangles until a box becomes pure, gets too small, or reaches the depth limit.

Tree Stopping Rules

To prevent the tree from growing infinitely, we define stopping constraints (hyperparameters in ML frameworks):

Node Purity: Stop if all items in a node belong to a single class (Gini = 0).
Max Depth (`max_depth`): Stop if the path length from the root matches our limit.
Min Samples Split (`min_samples_split`): Stop if a node contains too few samples to allow another split.
Min Samples Leaf (`min_samples_leaf`): Prevent splits that leave a child with too few samples.
Min Impurity Decrease (`min_impurity_decrease`): Stop if Gini gain is below a small threshold.
STOPPING RULES QUIZ

What is the main danger of growing a classification tree completely unchecked without any stopping rules?

The tree will underfit and fail to capture simple boundaries.
The tree will overfit by creating hyper-specific rules to capture training noise.
The root Gini impurity will increase beyond 0.50.
STAGE 08 · BUILD
The Decision Boundary

Once the tree stops growing, we fill in the colors. Each rectangular box becomes a "Leaf Node". The model assigns a prediction to the entire box based on the fruit type that appears most often in that box.

Leaf Nodes: How Predictions Are Made

Every final sub-box is a terminal Leaf Node. It predicts the majority class contained within its boundary.

We can also calculate a Class Probability Estimate simply as the proportion of that class in the leaf box:

P(Apple) = Leaf_Apples / Total_Leaf_Samples

⚠️ Warning: These leaf-proportion probabilities can be overconfident, especially in deep trees with small sample sizes in leaf boxes (e.g. predicting 100% confidence because a leaf contains exactly 1 Apple).

STAGE 09 · BUILD
Depth Limiting vs. Post-Pruning

Look closely at the tiny boxes the tree made just to capture one outlier fruit. The tree has started memorizing noise in the training dataset. This is called Overfitting.

If we give the tree new fruit, these hyper-specific rules will likely fail. We fix this by limiting the maximum depth of the tree (Pre-Pruning), so it learns general rules instead of tracking every detail.

Pre-Pruning vs. Post-Pruning
METHOD	HOW IT WORKS	PROS / CONS
Pre-Pruning	Stop tree growth early using rules like max_depth or min_samples_split.	Very fast to compute, but might stop too early before discovering complex interactions.
Post-Pruning	Grow the full complex tree first, then cut back nodes that do not add predictive value (e.g. cost-complexity pruning).	Often more systematic, but computationally heavier because you build the full tree first.

STAGE 15 · REFLECT
Limitations & Model Choice

Classification Trees are incredibly intuitive, but they are not always the best tool for every job. Understanding their trade-offs is crucial for a data scientist.

Strengths vs. Weaknesses
When they shine:
Explainability: Outputs simple rules that any non-expert can read and audit.
No Scaling Required: Features are evaluated independently, so feature magnitude does not matter.
Handles Mixed Types Conceptually: Trees can split numerical and categorical predictors, but raw categorical support depends on the software. Some libraries require encoded categories; others implement native categorical splits.
When they struggle:
High Variance: Extremely sensitive to tiny training set alterations, which can yield completely different splits.
Axis-Aligned Boundaries: Since splits are purely horizontal or vertical, diagonal patterns require jagged, inefficient steps.
Overfitting: Easily memorize noise if depth is unchecked.
Class Imbalance: If one class is much more common, the tree may favor that class unless class weights, resampling, or better evaluation metrics are used.
Model Comparison Roadmap
MODEL	BOUNDARY TYPE	INTERPRETABILITY	BEST USED FOR...
Decision Tree	Axis-Aligned Boxes	High (Flowchart)	Rules-based audits, mixed categorical/numerical data.
Logistic Regression	Smooth Linear	Medium (Weights)	Linear associations, computing well-calibrated odds.
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)	Irregular / Local	Low (Instance-based)	Complex local shapes, feature manifolds.
Random Forest	Complex / Smooth	Low (Ensemble)	High-accuracy, non-linear tasks (reduces variance).

🚀 The Upgrade Path: To overcome the instability and high variance of a single Classification Tree, we combine hundreds of trees into an ensemble. Models like Random Forests (voting trees) and Gradient Boosted Trees (sequential error correction) represent the state-of-the-art for tabular data!

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Probabilities, leakage, and honest pruning

A leaf probability is the class proportion among training cases in that leaf. Small leaves can produce unstable probabilities, so minimum-leaf constraints and calibration may matter.

All pruning and hyperparameter choices must use training or validation data only. Letting the test set influence tree depth is data leakage wearing a respectable-looking branch costume.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Each split should improve class purity enough to justify additional complexity.
Depth limits and pruning reduce overfitting.
Interpret both the decision path and out-of-sample metrics.

PRACTICAL METHOD CHECKLIST

Before you finish
Assumptions

When the method fails

Small leaves, unstable splits, conflicting labels, and distribution shift.

Validation and leakage

Choose depth and pruning through validation or cross-validation.

Interpretation cautions

Impurity, probabilities, and categorical support depend on context and software.

What to report

Tree constraints, pruning rule, class metrics with uncertainty, and final test result.

Hierarchical Clustering

The secret art of discovering hidden family trees in your data. No labels, no pre-defined answers—just the mathematical pursuit of "closeness".

SCROLL TO BEGIN
STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Uncharted Planet
BEFORE YOU START

Hierarchical clustering requires a distance measure and a linkage rule. Both choices define what it means for groups to be close.

Imagine landing on a distant planet with no map or guidebook. Your goal isn't to reach a destination; it's simply to see what is there. This is the essence of Unsupervised Learning.

Unlike supervised learning, where we try to predict a specific answer, here we only have features. We are discovering the natural structure of the data.

The Toy Box Analogy: Think of a child given a massive box of mixed toys and told to "find the patterns." Without instructions, they group them naturally by similarity.

To the right, we have a raw dataset. Just points in space waiting to be understood.

Takeaway: Unsupervised learning is about revealing structure that is already hiding in the data.

STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
Measuring "Close"

Before we can group anything, we must define what "similar" means. The most common way is to measure the physical distance between data points.

We use the Euclidean distance (the straight-line distance) to find out who is closest to whom. It is common, but not the only option; Manhattan, cosine, or domain-specific distances can make more sense for different data.

d(A, B) = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ]

By measuring the distance between every single pair of points, we build a "distance matrix"—a lookup table for similarity.

Takeaway: Clustering depends on your distance choice, because "close" is a design decision.

STAGE 03 · BUILD
The First Merge

Hierarchical clustering (specifically the Agglomerative or "bottom-up" kind) starts with a simple rule:

Every point starts as its own separate cluster.
Find the two clusters that are closest together.
Merge them.

Watch as the algorithm scans all points, finds the single closest pair, and binds them into a new, single cluster.

Takeaway: Agglomerative clustering grows structure from the bottom up, one merge at a time.

STAGE 04 · BUILD

Linkage and distance are not interchangeable. Ward linkage is tied to Euclidean geometry and increases in within-cluster variance. Single linkage can chain; complete linkage favours compact groups; average linkage is a compromise. Dendrogram heights do not represent the same quantity for every method.

Defining Group Distance (Linkage)

Merging two individual points is easy. But how do you measure the distance between a single point and a group? Or between two groups?

This is called Linkage. The linkage method you choose changes the shape of the clusters.

Takeaway: Linkage is the rulebook for deciding which groups are "closest" once clusters start to grow.

STAGE 05 · UNDERSTAND
The Process in Motion

Now, the algorithm repeats the rule over and over. It constantly recalculates distances using the linkage method, finding the next closest pair of clusters, and merging them.

Slowly, tiny groups fuse into medium groups, which fuse into large groups. It only stops when everything becomes one giant family. Use the merge scrubber on the right to step through the history one merge at a time.

STAGE 06 · UNDERSTAND
The Family Tree (Dendrogram)

Instead of just looking at circles on a map, we can record the exact history of these merges in a tree structure called a Dendrogram.

As the points align at the bottom, watch the tree grow upwards. The vertical height of each branch is critical: it tells us exactly how far apart the two groups were when they merged.

Rule of thumb: A fusion low on the tree means the items were very similar. A fusion high up means they were quite different.

Takeaway: A dendrogram preserves the full merge history, and branch height tells you how costly each merge was.

STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
Cutting the Tree

What if you don't know how many clusters you need? That is the superpower of hierarchical clustering: you don't have to guess upfront.

By drawing a horizontal line across the dendrogram, you "cut" the branches. The number of vertical lines you intersect is your number of clusters (K).

How do you choose the cut? A good first strategy is to look for a big jump in merge height and cut just below it, because that often means the algorithm has started forcing together groups that were meaningfully different. If you want a more quantitative check, you can also compare several cuts with a metric such as silhouette score.

Takeaway: Choose cuts where the tree shows a natural separation, not just where a slider gives a convenient K.

STAGE 08 · EXPLORE
The Detective's Challenge

Clustering is subjective detective work. Because there is no "true" answer (no target variable Y), the results rely entirely on your choices.

The "Socks and Computers" Problem

If variables use different units or their raw scales should not control distance, scale them using training data only. When variables share meaningful units and variance differences matter, standardisation may be undesirable.

Furthermore, an outlier can distort the tree, pulling a group away from its true members just to accommodate the stranger.

Takeaway: Scaling and outliers can change the tree dramatically, so preprocessing matters.

STAGE 09 · REFLECT
Synthesis & Recap

Hierarchical clustering gives us a rich, explorable structure rather than a single flat answer. Let's compare it to the other famous method, K-Means:

FEATURE	HIERARCHICAL	K-MEANS
Setup	Pick K after	Pick K first
Output	Tree (Dendrogram)	Flat groups
Speed	Usually slower because it builds the full merge tree and repeatedly compares clusters	Faster

Final Advice: Never take one clustering result as absolute truth. Try different linkages and cut heights. If the same patterns emerge every time, you've found something truly interesting.

Takeaway: Hierarchical clustering is valuable when you want an explorable merge history, not just one fixed partition.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Scaling and cluster stability

Standardise features when their units differ, unless those units deliberately encode importance. Otherwise one large-scale variable can dominate every merge.

Dendrogram branches are descriptive, not automatically “true” clusters. Compare linkage choices, inspect stability, and use domain knowledge when selecting a cut height.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
The dendrogram records the order and distance of merges.
Linkage choice changes the geometry of the resulting groups.
Scaling and cut height must be justified, not selected because the picture looks pleasant.

PRACTICAL METHOD CHECKLIST

Before you finish

A justified distance-linkage combination and meaningful feature scale.

When the method fails

Validation and leakage

Interpretation cautions

STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

LDA is a probabilistic classifier. It models each class and then compares posterior scores for a new observation.

Every machine learning model starts with data. Here we have measurements of fruits — each one scored on Sweetness and Color.

Each fruit is already labeled: it's either an Apple or an Orange. Because we have labels, this is supervised learning.

The Whole Idea of LDA

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a supervised classification method. It uses labeled examples to learn a straight-line rule that separates classes.

Simple Idea: LDA looks for a direction (projection axis) where:
• Different class centers are as far apart as possible.
• Points inside each class are as tightly bunched (low spread) as possible.

LDA General Pipeline:
Labeled Data → Class Centers → Class Spread → Optimal Direction → Boundary → Prediction

"LDA is like looking at a messy 2D cloud of points from the best angle so the two groups look as separated as possible."

Tiny LDA Dictionary
Feature: A measurement used to make a prediction (e.g., Sweetness or Color).
Label: The known category of an example (e.g., Apple or Orange).
Class: The target group we want to predict (Apple class or Orange class).
Mean (μ): The average position or center of a class point cloud.
Variance: How much a single feature fluctuates.
Covariance: How two features move in relation to each other.
Scatter (S): A mathematical measure of data spread or messiness.
Projection: Squashing 2D coordinates down onto a single 1D axis.
Discriminant Score (δ): A numerical score LDA computes for each class; the highest score wins!

STAGE 09 · UNDERSTAND
The Optimal Direction

In this 2-class example, LDA gives one main discriminant direction w — the angle where classes appear most separated.

What is projection and why do we do it?

Projection means dropping every 2D point (Sweetness, Color) down onto a single 1D line or direction.

This turns a 2D pair of numbers into a single 1D score:

Fruit (Sweetness, Color) → [Project] → One LDA Score

Why project? If the projected Apple scores sit neatly on one side of the line and the projected Orange scores sit on the other side, LDA has found an excellent direction for separation!

w ∝ S_W⁻¹ (μ₁ − μ₂)

This isn't just the straight line between means.
It also tilts to avoid the direction of maximum within-class spread.
Optimal Direction w
w = S_W⁻¹ · (μ₁ − μ₂) → [ 0.4594, 0.8883 ]

This direction maximizes the Fisher criterion J(w). Points projected onto it show maximum class separation.

STAGE 14 · PREPARE
Assumptions & Limitations

To use LDA effectively, you need to understand when it thrives and when it falls short.

LDA Works Best When:
Linearity: A straight-line boundary is a reasonable way to separate classes.
Normality: Each class looks like a symmetrical oval cloud (multivariate normal distribution).
Equal Spread: All classes share roughly the same spread/covariance shape.
Independence: Data samples are collected independently.
Data Volume: There are many more rows than features.
No Outliers: Extreme values are absent (outliers pull means away easily).
LDA Struggles When:
The true dividing boundary is highly curved.
Classes have very different shapes or spreads (e.g., one is a tight circle, the other is a giant flat ellipse).
There are severe outliers that skew centers.
You have too many features and not enough rows (overfitting).
Features are redundant or highly correlated (collinearity).
Alternative Methods

If LDA doesn't fit, consider these standard alternatives:

🎯 QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis): Excellent if class spreads are highly unequal.
📈 Logistic Regression: Better if you need direct probabilities and fewer statistical assumptions.
🌲 KNN or Decision Trees: Great for highly complex, non-linear boundaries.
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Posterior probabilities and regularised LDA

The discriminant scores can be converted into posterior class probabilities. These probabilities are useful for ranking and threshold decisions, not merely producing a hard label.

When the covariance estimate is unstable because there are many features or limited data, shrinkage or regularised LDA can trade a little bias for much lower variance.

The Whole Idea of QDA

Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) is a supervised classification method. It models each class as its own independent multi-dimensional probability cloud.

Simple intuition: QDA asks: "Which of these distinct class clouds does this new coordinate fit into best?"

Unlike LDA (which forces every class to share the exact same shape), QDA allows each class to have its own unique spread, stretch, and tilt. This mathematical flexibility is what creates curved boundaries.

QDA Pipeline: Labeled data → Split Train/Test → Fit class-specific shapes → Score new test coordinates → Make prediction → Evaluate performance

The Overfitting Trap
BEFORE YOU START

Model selection is part of model fitting. Every candidate comparison must be contained inside the training or cross-validation process.

Building a predictive model is tricky. It is tempting to include every available piece of data. We often assume that more clues guarantee better answers.

However, adding too many variables introduces massive noise. This noise obscures the true relationship. The model ends up memorizing random accidents in the training data rather than learning the actual signal.

The Illusion of Accuracy: A highly complex model performs flawlessly on its "homework" (the training data). But it collapses in the real world on unseen data. This failure is called overfitting.

STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
The n-p Puzzle

To build a reliable model, we must balance two things. First is the number of samples (

Think of this in three simple steps:

Step 1: You need enough examples to prove a real pattern exists.
Step 2: Every new variable adds a whole new dimension for the model to search.
Step 3: When

At this point, the design matrix is rank deficient. Without additional constraints, many coefficient vectors may fit the training data equally well. This makes coefficient interpretation unstable and creates a high risk of overfitting. Useful prediction may still be possible with appropriate regularisation, feature structure and honest validation.

Keep the ideas separate: non-unique coefficients concern identifiability; interpolation means matching the observed training outcomes; overfitting is poor generalisation caused by learning sample-specific patterns; predictive performance must be measured on unseen data. Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net impose different constraints that can produce estimable predictors, but they are not automatic cures.

STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
Picking the Best Team

One way to fix this is Subset Selection. This means literally picking a specific group of variables and throwing the rest out.

FORWARD Start empty. Add the single best predictor. Then add the next one that helps the most. Keep going.

BACKWARD Start with all variables. Find the weakest predictor and bench them. Repeat until only the best are left.

HYBRID Add the best predictors one by one. But constantly re-evaluate. If an old predictor becomes redundant, remove it.

The "Super-Variable" Secret

If we have 100 highly correlated variables, they provide redundant information. Dimension Reduction allows us to "squish" them into a few super-variables called Principal Components.

Compress first, predict later. It squishes variables together without looking at what you are trying to predict.

STAGE 11 · REFLECT
Common Mistakes

Even advanced statistical methods are not magic. Here is how to avoid common traps.

MISTAKE 1

Choosing a model based on training accuracy.

CORRECT PRACTICE

Always compare and judge models based on cross-validation error. Training accuracy is always overly optimistic.

MISTAKE 2

Testing on the final test set multiple times.

CORRECT PRACTICE

Lock the final test set in a vault. Use it only once at the very end to check your final model. If you use it to tweak parameters, it is no longer an honest test.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Prefer the simplest near-best model

Validation scores contain noise. The one-standard-error rule chooses the simplest model whose performance is within one standard error of the best observed score.

When comparing many pipelines, use nested cross-validation or a final untouched test set. Otherwise the “best” model may simply be the one that benefited most from repeated checking.

STAGE 12 · REFLECT
Final Synthesis

We do not want a model that is too simple (underfitting). We do not want a model that is too dramatic (overfitting).

By using Cross-Validation, we compare and validate models fairly. By applying Regularization or Subset Selection, we penalize messiness and force the model to focus only on what matters.

The ultimate goal is Generalization. We want to build a model that stays trustworthy and useful when reality shows up and starts ruining everyone's assumptions.

FINAL CHECK

To achieve 0% error on the training data.
Generalization: performing well on unseen real-world data.

Ridge keeps all predictors; Lasso can set some coefficients to zero.

STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
Points, labels, and a decision boundary

Each point is one labelled training row with two features. Colour marks the class. A classifier needs a rule that places a future point on one side or the other.

f(x) > 0  →  Class +1
f(x) < 0  →  Class −1

In two dimensions the boundary is a line. In three dimensions it is a plane. Beyond that, it becomes a hyperplane, a dramatic name for the same separating idea.

The plot uses two features because humans remain tragically dependent on visible space. The model itself can work with many features.
STAGE 02 · QUESTION
Why not choose any separating line?

When the classes are separable, several lines can classify every training point correctly. Training accuracy alone cannot tell us which line is safer.

Narrow clearance

Fits the training rows, but a small measurement change can flip a prediction.

Wide clearance

Leaves more room before the nearest point crosses the boundary.

A linear SVM adds a preference: choose the separator with the greatest distance to the closest points from either class.

Quick check: what extra criterion does SVM use?
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
The margin is protected space

The margin is the gap between two parallel support planes touching the closest training points on each side.

Boundary: wᵀx + b = 0
Margin boundaries: wᵀx + b = +1 and −1
Geometric margin width = 2 / ‖w‖

Maximising the margin is equivalent to keeping the weight vector small while still satisfying the classification constraints.

A wide margin can make the separator less sensitive. It cannot rescue biased data, leakage, poor labels, or a mismatched kernel. Geometry is useful, not divine intervention.
STAGE 04 · FOCUS
Support vectors are the points that matter most

Support vectors lie on or inside the margin. They directly constrain the fitted boundary.

f(x) = Σᵢ αᵢ yᵢ K(xᵢ, x) + b
Only rows with αᵢ > 0 are support vectors.

Move a distant, safely classified point a little and the boundary may not change. Move a support vector and the solution can shift immediately.

Important distinction: “support vector” means the row constrains this fitted margin. It does not mean the row is causally or commercially important in every possible sense.
STAGE 05 · RELAX
Hard margins break when reality overlaps

A hard-margin SVM demands perfect separation with every row outside the margin. Real classes overlap, labels contain errors, and outliers appear because datasets enjoy sabotage.

A soft-margin SVM introduces slack variables ξᵢ so violations are allowed but penalised.

yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 − ξᵢ,  with ξᵢ ≥ 0
SLACK	MEANING
ξ = 0	Correct and on or beyond the margin
0 < ξ ≤ 1	Correct side, but inside the margin
ξ > 1	Misclassified
STAGE 06 · TUNE
C decides how expensive violations are
minimise  ½‖w‖² + C Σᵢ ξᵢ
Small C

Violations are cheaper. The model accepts more errors to preserve a wider, smoother margin.

Large C

Violations are expensive. The model fits training rows more aggressively, often with a narrower margin.

C is an inverse regularisation parameter: larger C means less regularisation.

A huge C does not mean “more accurate”. It means “punish training violations more”, which can also mean “memorise the noise with confidence”.
STAGE 07 · PREPARE
Scale features before comparing distances

SVM geometry uses dot products and distances. A feature ranging from 0 to 100,000 can dominate another ranging from 0 to 1, even when the smaller-scale feature is genuinely informative.

standardised value = (value − training mean) ÷ training standard deviation

Fit the scaler inside each training fold, then apply that fitted transformation to validation, test, and production rows.

Two distinct failures: scaling before the split leaks information; scaling the test set separately changes the coordinate system. Both are wrong in impressively different ways.
STAGE 08 · FORMALISE
Hinge loss ignores easy correct points
hinge loss = max(0, 1 − y × f(x))
SIGNED MARGIN Y F(X)	LOSS	INTERPRETATION
≥ 1	0	Correct and safely beyond the margin
0 to 1	positive	Correct but inside the margin
≤ 0	≥ 1	Misclassified

Once a point is correctly beyond the margin, its hinge loss is zero. Distant easy points stop pulling the boundary.

STAGE 09 · INTERPRET
The decision score is not automatically a probability

The decision function reports which side of the boundary a row occupies and how strongly it lies in that direction.

larger positive f(x) → stronger Class +1 decision
larger negative f(x) → stronger Class −1 decision

For a linear SVM, the score relates to signed distance after accounting for ‖w‖. For a kernel SVM, treat it as a boundary score rather than literal distance in the original plot.

f(x) = 2 does not mean 200%, nor twice the probability of f(x) = 1. Probability estimates require a separate calibration model fitted with held-out predictions.
STAGE 10 · EXTEND
A straight boundary cannot solve every pattern

Imagine one class forming an inner cluster and another forming an outer ring. No straight line can separate them in the original two-feature space.

A transformed feature such as squared radius can reveal the structure:

r² = x₁² + x₂²

In transformed space, a simple threshold on r² can separate inner from outer points. A curved boundary in the original plot can still correspond to a linear rule elsewhere.

STAGE 11 · KERNELISE
The kernel trick avoids explicit feature explosion

A kernel computes similarities that behave like inner products in a richer feature space, without explicitly constructing every transformed coordinate.

K(x, z) = φ(x)ᵀφ(z)

RBF: K(x,z) = exp(−γ ‖x − z‖²)
Small gamma

Each point has broad influence. The decision surface changes slowly.

Large gamma

Influence becomes local. The boundary can wrap tightly around training points.

Large gamma plus large C can create an intricate boundary that remembers noise instead of learning structure.

A regression tree predicts a number by averaging training outcomes within a terminal leaf. The fitted function is therefore piecewise constant.

A regression tree is a model that helps us predict a number. Not a category like "cat or dog", but a continuous value like an exam score, temperature, or a house price.

STAGE 15 · REFLECT
Reality Check: Limitations

While extremely powerful and explainable, single regression trees have key engineering limitations that you must look out for in practice.

🚫 Poor Extrapolation
Trend Fail

Trees predict flat averages. If a house size is larger than any seen in training (e.g., 220 m²), the tree cannot continue a trend upward; it flatlines at the average of the largest leaf.

📈 Jagged Step Predictions
Staircase

Real-world factors often rise smoothly. Trees build staircases with sudden step jumps, struggling to cleanly represent smooth curves without huge depths.

⚡ High Instability (Variance)
High Variance

A tiny shift in data (e.g., swapping one point's price) can completely re-arrange the root split boundary, producing a highly unstable prediction layout.

📐 Axis-Aligned Splits
Orthogonal

Basic trees split one feature at a time at right angles, making it difficult to capture diagonal correlations (like price dropping when size decreases and age increases simultaneously).

🕸️ Easy to Overfit
High Complexity

Without strict stopping rules or pruning, deep trees will easily grow until they isolate every single point, memorizing individual training points instead of discovering generalizable patterns.

Synthesis

Let's review the final sequence to build and use a regression tree:

1.
Put all training data in the Root Node.
2.
Test possible splits (greedy thresholds) across all available features.
3.
Pick the feature/split that results in the lowest RSS.
4.
Repeat the process recursively inside each new branch.
5.
Use validation error to choose stopping rules or pruning, instead of trusting training error alone.
6.
Each final leaf predicts the average target value inside that leaf.

While a single regression tree can be unstable on its own, this recursive logic is the fundamental building block for advanced modern algorithms like Random Forests and Gradient Boosting.

Ensemble Learning: Ensembles improve single trees by combining hundreds of them, smoothing out jagged steps and yielding highly stable predictions.
COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Extrapolation and uncertainty

A regression tree cannot naturally extrapolate a trend beyond the training range. New extreme values usually inherit the prediction of the outermost leaf.

Single-tree predictions can be unstable. Ensembles such as random forests or gradient boosting reduce variance, while conformal or bootstrap methods can add uncertainty estimates when required.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Splits are chosen to reduce within-node squared error.
Pruning trades a little training fit for better generalisation.
Trees capture interactions and nonlinearities but predict in steps and extrapolate poorly.

Define the finish line

Deep learning starts with a decision, not a network. You first describe the real task in a way that can be demonstrated with examples and measured with evidence.

WHY IT MATTERS

A vague goal such as “recognise animals” leaves too many questions unanswered. Should the model find every animal, draw a box around it, or choose one label? Clear boundaries determine the data you need, the output layer you build, and the mistakes you measure.

2

3

BUILD THE EVIDENCE

Collect reality, not shortcuts

A dataset is the model’s entire experience of the world. It will use any regular pattern that helps, whether that pattern expresses the true idea or an accidental shortcut.

WHY IT MATTERS

If every dog is photographed on grass and every cat is photographed on a sofa, “background” becomes an easier clue than “animal.” The model can score well in the lab and fail immediately in a real home, park, shelter, or veterinary clinic.

HOW IT WORKS
1

Collect variation in lighting, background, angle, distance, appearance, position, and image quality.

2

Inspect examples by class and source; look for rare classes, duplicate files, broken records, and inconsistent labels.

3

Ask what unrelated clue could reveal the answer. Then deliberately collect counterexamples that break that shortcut.

Picture it: A child shown only red apples may decide that “apple” means “red.” Variation teaches which features stay true when the scenery changes.

More examples help only when they add useful coverage. Ten thousand copies of the same narrow situation are still narrow data.

Split before you tune

WHY IT MATTERS

When the model—or the people tuning it—repeatedly sees the final test answers, the score stops measuring generalisation. Duplicate images, the same patient in two splits, or future data leaking into the past can create confidence without real ability.

HOW IT WORKS
1

Use training data to update weights and validation data to compare choices, tune settings, and decide when to stop.

2

Seal the test set until the architecture and meaningful choices are fixed, then use it once for the final estimate.

3

Keep related people, videos, devices, or time periods together, and learn preprocessing statistics from training data only.

One artificial neuron is a small decision-maker. It combines several signals into one new signal that later neurons can use.

Depth builds features

A deep network turns the same example into a sequence of increasingly useful descriptions. Each layer receives the previous layer’s features and composes them into larger ideas.

WHY IT MATTERS

Raw pixels are a poor language for “dog.” Edges are more useful; groups of edges can describe fur or curves; those patterns can form ears, eyes, and snouts. Hierarchy lets the model reuse simple discoveries to build complex ones.

Early layers respond to local changes such as edges, colour transitions, or short sound patterns.

2

3

Later layers gather evidence across a wider area and make features useful for the final task.

THE CORRECTION CYCLE

How learning happens

Learning is a repeated correction loop. The network guesses, measures how wrong it was, works out which parameters influenced the mistake, and makes a small adjustment.

WHY IT MATTERS

A loss number alone says only “this was wrong.” Backpropagation turns that complaint into useful directions for millions of parameters, allowing each one to change in proportion to its contribution.

HOW IT WORKS
1

Forward propagation moves a batch through the layers and produces predictions.

2

A loss function compares predictions with the correct answers; backpropagation calculates gradients from output to input.

3

An optimiser uses those gradients to update the weights. The learning rate controls how large each step is.

Picture it: Imagine descending a foggy hill. The gradient tells you which way slopes downward; the learning rate decides whether you take careful steps or dangerous leaps.

One update teaches very little. Useful behaviour emerges from many batches of examples providing many small, partly noisy corrections.

An architecture is a set of useful assumptions about how information is organised. The right design makes important patterns easier and cheaper to learn.

WHY IT MATTERS

Images contain many local patterns, not one universal feature. Sequences need memory or direct links across time. Architecture decides how information is shared, how far context can travel, and what the model can compute efficiently.

2

An RNN reads one item at a time and updates a hidden state—a fixed-length vector that compresses what it has seen. That state can produce scores for the next word or another sequence output.

3

A Transformer creates a query, key, and value for every token. Query–key matches become attention weights, which gather useful values into context. Training rewards links that help reduce prediction error.

Transfer learning starts from a model that has already learned general patterns from a large dataset, then adapts that knowledge to your narrower task.

Training a large network from random weights can require enormous amounts of labelled data and computation. Useful early features—edges, textures, shapes, language patterns—often transfer between related tasks.

Evaluation asks not only “how often is it right?” but “where, for whom, and with what confidence does it fail?” The final test set estimates performance on genuinely unseen data.

A model can reach 95% accuracy by always predicting the common class in an imbalanced dataset. In medicine, fraud, or safety, one missed positive can matter far more than one false alarm.

Plain-English translation: examples go in, a prediction comes out, mistakes are measured, and the internal settings are adjusted so the next prediction is less wrong.

Normal programming versus machine learning

Normal programming: a human writes the rules, the computer applies them, and an answer comes out. Machine learning: a human supplies examples and correct outcomes, then the model learns useful rules from those examples. Neural networks are valuable when the rules are too numerous or complicated to write by hand.

BEFORE YOU CONTINUE

You only need basic comfort with multiplication, averages, and percentages. Every specialist word is defined before it is used.

Data becomes features and labels

Data is the collection of examples the model learns from. In our toy problem, each row describes one student.

Supervised learning means the training examples already contain the correct answers. Features are the clues; the label is the answer key.

STAGE 03
Clean, encode, scale, then split

Real data is rarely ready to train on. Missing values, duplicates, impossible values, inconsistent labels, and suspicious outliers must be investigated before the model sees them.

1. Clean

Fix or remove records that are missing, duplicated, impossible, or inconsistent.

2. Encode

Turn words and categories into numbers because the network performs mathematics.

3. Scale

Put numerical features on comparable ranges so a large unit does not look important merely because its number is bigger.

4. Split

Keep separate training, validation, and test sets so memorization cannot impersonate learning.

Training set   ≈ 70%  → teaches the model
Validation set ≈ 15%  → tunes choices during development
Test set       ≈ 15%  → final, untouched exam

Keep the final exam separate: the test examples must not be used to teach or tune the model. Otherwise the final score no longer shows how well the model handles genuinely unseen data.

A feature measured in thousands can dominate numerical updates even when it is not more meaningful.

What it does not mean

Scaling does not automatically decide which feature matters. The network still learns weights from the data.

ReLU is a learned-pattern gate. A positive raw score passes as evidence that one learned pattern is present; zero means that neuron does not pass evidence for that pattern. STAGE 07
Forward propagation makes one pass-score prediction

Forward propagation means information moves from the three inputs, through every hidden layer, to the single output neuron used by this binary task.

For one student, the output neuron might produce 0.82. We read that as an 82% model score for “pass.” The corresponding fail score is 1 − 0.82 = 0.18.

The output neuron does not yet make the final Pass/Fail decision. Stage 14 will apply a separate decision threshold, such as 0.50, to turn this continuous score into a class label.

STAGE 08
Loss measures how wrong the prediction was

A loss function converts prediction error into a number. Smaller loss is better. Larger loss tells the training process that the current weights need more correction.

Regression

When predicting a number, mean squared error is common. It squares mistakes, so large errors receive extra punishment.

Classification

When predicting a class, cross-entropy loss is common. It strongly penalizes a model that is confidently wrong.

!

Loss is the teacher's marking pen. It does not merely say “wrong.” It gives the optimizer a numerical signal showing how much improvement is needed.

DO NOT CONFUSE THESE

Loss versus metric
Loss

The quantity optimized during training. It guides weight updates.

Metric

A human-readable measure such as accuracy, precision, recall, MAE, or RMSE.

STAGE 09
Backpropagation computes gradients—only gradients

A gradient is a collection of slopes: for each weight, it answers “if this weight increased a tiny amount, how would the loss change?” The sign gives a direction and the magnitude describes local sensitivity.

forward pass → prediction
prediction + truth → loss
backpropagation → gradient for every weight and bias
weights are still unchanged

Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss backward through the network. It calculates how local changes connect to the final error. It does not choose a learning rate and it never updates a parameter.

Plain distinction: backprop computes gradients only. The optimizer later uses those gradients to update weights.

STAGE 10
The optimizer takes iterative, local steps

Gradient descent applies the update. It combines the local gradient with a learning rate: next weight = current weight − learning rate × gradient. Because the gradient describes only the slope near the current point, optimization must repeat rather than jump directly to the answer.

STAGE 12
Choose the model before validation gets worse

Training loss can keep falling while validation loss eventually rises. That is the causal signature of overfitting: the model is improving on examples it trains on while becoming less useful on unseen data. Keep the checkpoint near the lowest validation loss, not the final training step.

STAGE 16
Saving, deployment, and monitoring finish the lifecycle

Once performance is acceptable, the final model is saved. The saved package includes the architecture, learned weights and biases, and often the preprocessing rules needed to reproduce training-time inputs.

→ saved model
→ prediction
→ application response

Deployment puts the model into a website, mobile app, server API, edge device, or business system. A model sitting in a notebook is an experiment, not a working service.

AFTER LAUNCH

Monitor accuracy, error types, input-data changes, speed, complaints, fairness, and security. When the world changes and performance falls, the model is experiencing drift.

STAGE 17
Different network families organize information differently
Feedforward network

Information moves from input to hidden layers to output. This is the structure used throughout this lesson.

Convolutional network (CNN)

Common for images. Early layers notice edges; later layers combine them into shapes and object parts.

Recurrent network (RNN)

Designed for sequences and previous context, such as text, audio, and time series.

Transformer

Uses attention to connect relevant parts of data, allowing many relationships to be considered at once.

This layered transformation is called representation learning. Raw inputs become increasingly useful internal patterns: pixels → edges → shapes → objects, or word pieces → phrases → context.

Interpretability: weights are visible, but a representation is usually distributed across many parameters. Inspecting one large weight rarely yields a faithful human rule; use case-level explanations, sensitivity analyses, and validation evidence together.

Neural networks are powerful because they can learn complex representations. They are used for images, speech, text, translation, recommendations, medical scans, fraud detection, forecasting, game playing, and large language models. They are not magic: they still depend on good data, sensible design, testing, monitoring, and human judgment.

STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
The Spurious Trap

If multiple variables just stack, why not run a simple regression for each variable separately? Because of Spurious Correlations.

Imagine we want to predict Shark Attacks. If we run a simple model using Ice Cream Sales, the correlation is huge! It looks like ice cream causes shark attacks.

But the true driver is a lurking variable: High Temperature. Hot days cause both ice cream sales and beach visits (which lead to shark attacks).

The Power of "Holding Constant"
Multiple regression isolates a variable's unique contribution, which can reveal when a variable only looked important because it moved together with another predictor. If we put both Ice Cream and Temperature into the model, the model essentially compares days with the same temperature. Holding temperature constant, changing ice cream sales alone has almost zero unique effect on shark attacks.

If a coefficient shrinks close to zero after the other predictors are included, that suggests it has little unique relationship with the predicted outcome (y) after accounting for the others. This does not prove the variable has no real-world effect at all, only that it adds little unique information within this specific model.

Note: A larger coefficient doesn't always mean a "more important" predictor, as they depend on the unit of measurement.

STAGE 08 · REFLECT
The Adjusted R² Penalty

How do we know if our team of variables is actually good? R² tells us what percentage of the variance we explained.

But raw R² has a flaw: it almost never goes down when you add predictors. Adding any variable—even "Student's Shoe Size"—will mathematically force raw R² to increase, tricking you into thinking the model is better.

Adj R² = 1 - [ (1 - R²)(n - 1) / (n - p - 1) ]

Adjusted R² corrects for this by penalizing model complexity. In the formula, n is the number of observations and p is the number of predictors.

Every new predictor (p) uses up flexibility and increases the penalty. A new variable should only stay if it improves the model enough to justify its cost. A useless variable will cause Adjusted R² to stay flat or drop!

When a data analyst fits a multiple linear regression, they don't look at a 3D plot—they look at a summary table to evaluate the results.

Estimate:
The coefficient (β). How much the prediction changes for a one-unit increase in this predictor, holding all other predictors constant.
Std. Error:
The uncertainty around the estimate. A smaller standard error means we are more confident in the coefficient.
t value:
The estimate divided by its standard error. A larger absolute value (typically > 2) indicates strong statistical evidence that the true effect is not zero.

Note: Each coefficient should be read as "the change in predicted y for a one-unit increase in this predictor, holding the others constant." Because predictors can be measured in entirely different units, coefficients cannot be compared as pure "importance scores" unless the predictors are on comparable scales.

Diagnostics belong with the output. Inspect residual-versus-fitted, Q–Q, scale-location, leverage and influence plots. Use VIFs and coefficient intervals to diagnose multicollinearity; document categorical reference levels and interactions. Report confidence intervals for mean responses and wider prediction intervals for new observations. These coefficients are adjusted associations, not causal effects without a causal design.
Multiple linear regression is a powerful detective. It models additive effects, isolates individual drivers, and finds the mathematically optimal fit by minimizing squared errors.

Each coefficient describes a partial relationship while the other predictors are held constant.

The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

A classification tree repeatedly divides the feature space into regions. Each terminal leaf predicts a class or class probability.

Each fruit is already labeled: an Apple or an Orange. The goal of our tree is to learn rules to sort them into cleaner groups.

 The Whole Idea of Classification Trees

A Classification Tree is a supervised machine-learning model that learns a sequence of simple yes/no flowchart-like questions to sort data into categories.

Raw Labeled Data → Root Node → Scan Best Question → Split Data → Repeat Recursively → Leaf Prediction → Evaluation
 Tiny Tree Dictionary
• Feature: A measurable property or input variable used to make predictions (e.g., Weight, Color Intensity).
• Label: The target outcome or true answer we want the model to predict (e.g., Apple, Orange).
• Class: One of the specific categorical outcomes (e.g., Apples vs. Oranges).
• Root Node: The very first top-level block containing 100% of the training data.
• Split: A division of a parent node into two child nodes based on a feature question.
• Child Node: The subgroups created after splitting a parent node.
• Leaf Node: A final terminal node that does not split further. It makes the final prediction.
• Impurity: A measure of how mixed or diverse the class labels are within a particular node.
• Gini Impurity: A mathematical metric used to calculate impurity (0.0 means perfectly pure; 0.5 is the maximum for a balanced binary node).
• Weighted Impurity: The combined impurity of child nodes, weighted by the proportion of samples that went into each child.
• Impurity Decrease: The difference between parent Gini and weighted child Gini. The tree maximizes this "gain".
• Decision Boundary: The geometric line(s) dividing different class zones on the coordinate map.
• Tree Depth: The length of the longest path from the root node down to any leaf node.
• Pruning: Cutting back branches to simplify the model and improve generalizability on unseen data.
• Overfitting: Memorizing noise in the training set, causing failure on unseen test data.
• Underfitting: Creating a model that is too simple (e.g. too shallow) to learn the real underlying patterns.

To split effectively, the tree needs a way to measure how mixed a box is. We use a math rule called Gini Impurity.

How does a decision tree find the best threshold? It doesn't guess random decimals. Instead, it uses a deterministic mathematical process:

Sort values: For a given feature (like Weight), it sorts all observed training values in ascending order.
Compute Midpoints: It calculates the halfway points (midpoints) between every adjacent pair of unique values.
Evaluate Splits: It treats each midpoint as a candidate threshold (e.g., Weight < 5.40), splits the data, and evaluates the resulting weighted Gini impurity.

To prevent the tree from growing infinitely, we define stopping constraints (hyperparameters in ML frameworks):

Node Purity: Stop if all items in a node belong to a single class (Gini = 0).
Max Depth (`max_depth`): Stop if the path length from the root matches our limit.
Min Samples Split (`min_samples_split`): Stop if a node contains too few samples to allow another split.
Min Samples Leaf (`min_samples_leaf`): Prevent splits that leave a child with too few samples.
Min Impurity Decrease (`min_impurity_decrease`): Stop if Gini gain is below a small threshold.

Classification Trees are incredibly intuitive, but they are not always the best tool for every job. Understanding their trade-offs is crucial for a data scientist.

 Strengths vs.  Weaknesses
When they shine:

STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Uncharted Planet
BEFORE YOU START

Hierarchical clustering requires a distance measure and a linkage rule. Both choices define what it means for groups to be close.

Imagine landing on a distant planet with no map or guidebook. Your goal isn't to reach a destination; it's simply to see what is there. This is the essence of Unsupervised Learning.

Unlike supervised learning, where we try to predict a specific answer, here we only have features. We are discovering the natural structure of the data.

The Toy Box Analogy: Think of a child given a massive box of mixed toys and told to "find the patterns." Without instructions, they group them naturally by similarity.

To the right, we have a raw dataset. Just points in space waiting to be understood.

Takeaway: Unsupervised learning is about revealing structure that is already hiding in the data.

STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
Measuring "Close"

Before we can group anything, we must define what "similar" means. The most common way is to measure the physical distance between data points.

We use the Euclidean distance (the straight-line distance) to find out who is closest to whom. It is common, but not the only option; Manhattan, cosine, or domain-specific distances can make more sense for different data.

d(A, B) = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ]

By measuring the distance between every single pair of points, we build a "distance matrix"—a lookup table for similarity.

Takeaway: Clustering depends on your distance choice, because "close" is a design decision.

STAGE 03 · BUILD
The First Merge

Hierarchical clustering (specifically the Agglomerative or "bottom-up" kind) starts with a simple rule:

Every point starts as its own separate cluster.
Find the two clusters that are closest together.
Merge them.

Watch as the algorithm scans all points, finds the single closest pair, and binds them into a new, single cluster.

Takeaway: Agglomerative clustering grows structure from the bottom up, one merge at a time.

STAGE 04 · BUILD

Single linkage can chain; complete linkage favours compact groups; average linkage is a compromise. Dendrogram heights do not represent the same quantity for every method.

Merging two individual points is easy. But how do you measure the distance between a single point and a group? Or between two groups?

This is called Linkage. The linkage method you choose changes the shape of the clusters.

The Family Tree (Dendrogram)

Instead of just looking at circles on a map, we can record the exact history of these merges in a tree structure called a Dendrogram.

As the points align at the bottom, watch the tree grow upwards. The vertical height of each branch is critical: it tells us exactly how far apart the two groups were when they merged.

STAGE 07 · UNDERSTAND
Cutting the Tree

What if you don't know how many clusters you need? That is the superpower of hierarchical clustering: you don't have to guess upfront.

By drawing a horizontal line across the dendrogram, you "cut" the branches. The number of vertical lines you intersect is your number of clusters (K).

How do you choose the cut? A good first strategy is to look for a big jump in merge height and cut just below it, because that often means the algorithm has started forcing together groups that were meaningfully different. The Detective's Challenge

Clustering is subjective detective work. Because there is no "true" answer (no target variable Y), the results rely entirely on your choices.

The "Socks and Computers" Problem

If variables use different units or their raw scales should not control distance, scale them using training data only. When variables share meaningful units and variance differences matter, standardisation may be undesirable.

Furthermore, an outlier can distort the tree, pulling a group away from its true members just to accommodate the stranger.

STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
The Raw Data
BEFORE YOU START

LDA is a probabilistic classifier. It models each class and then compares posterior scores for a new observation.

Every machine learning model starts with data. Here we have measurements of fruits — each one scored on Sweetness and Color.

Each fruit is already labeled: it's either an Apple or an Orange. Because we have labels, this is supervised learning.

The Whole Idea of LDA

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a supervised classification method. It uses labeled examples to learn a straight-line rule that separates classes.

Simple Idea: LDA looks for a direction (projection axis) where:
• Different class centers are as far apart as possible.
• Points inside each class are as tightly bunched (low spread) as possible.

LDA General Pipeline:
Labeled Data → Class Centers → Class Spread → Optimal Direction → Boundary → Prediction

"LDA is like looking at a messy 2D cloud of points from the best angle so the two groups look as separated as possible."

Tiny LDA Dictionary
Feature: A measurement used to make a prediction (e.g., Sweetness or Color).
Label: The known category of an example (e.g., Apple or Orange).
Class: The target group we want to predict (Apple class or Orange class).
Mean (μ): The average position or center of a class point cloud.
Variance: How much a single feature fluctuates.
Covariance: How two features move in relation to each other.
Scatter (S): A mathematical measure of data spread or messiness.
Projection: Squashing 2D coordinates down onto a single 1D axis.
Discriminant Score (δ): A numerical score LDA computes for each class; the highest score wins!

Covariance tells us whether Sweetness and Color move together:

Here's LDA's key assumption: all classes share the same covariance shape. The groups can have different centers, but their spread is assumed to be roughly the same.

In this 2-class example, LDA gives one main discriminant direction w — the angle where classes appear most separated.

What is projection and why do we do it?

Projection means dropping every 2D point (Sweetness, Color) down onto a single 1D line or direction.

This turns a 2D pair of numbers into a single 1D score:

Fruit (Sweetness, Color) → [Project] → One LDA Score

Why project? If the projected Apple scores sit neatly on one side of the line and the projected Orange scores sit on the other side, LDA has found an excellent direction for separation!

w ∝ S_W⁻¹ (μ₁ − μ₂)

This isn't just the straight line between means.
It also tilts to avoid the direction of maximum within-class spread.
Optimal Direction w
w = S_W⁻¹ · (μ₁ − μ₂) → [ 0.4594, 0.8883 ]

This direction maximizes the Fisher criterion J(w). Points projected onto it show maximum class separation.

LDA calculates a separate scoring function for each class, called the Discriminant Score (δ):

δ_apple(x) = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Apple
δ_orange(x) = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Orange

For any point, LDA compares the two scores: whichever score is higher is the predicted class!

Assumptions & Limitations

To use LDA effectively, you need to understand when it thrives and when it falls short.

LDA Works Best When:
Linearity: A straight-line boundary is a reasonable way to separate classes.
Normality: Each class looks like a symmetrical oval cloud (multivariate normal distribution).
Equal Spread: All classes share roughly the same spread/covariance shape.
Independence: Data samples are collected independently.
Data Volume: There are many more rows than features.
No Outliers: Extreme values are absent (outliers pull means away easily).
LDA Struggles When:
The true dividing boundary is highly curved.
Classes have very different shapes or spreads (e.g., one is a tight circle, the other is a giant flat ellipse).
There are severe outliers that skew centers.
You have too many features and not enough rows (overfitting).
Features are redundant or highly correlated (collinearity).
Alternative Methods

If LDA doesn't fit, consider these standard alternatives:

 QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis): Excellent if class spreads are highly unequal.
 Logistic Regression: Better if you need direct probabilities and fewer statistical assumptions.
 KNN or Decision Trees: Great for highly complex, non-linear boundaries.

The Whole Idea of QDA

Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) is a supervised classification method. It models each class as its own independent multi-dimensional probability cloud.

Simple intuition: QDA asks: "Which of these distinct class clouds does this new coordinate fit into best?"

Unlike LDA (which forces every class to share the exact same shape), QDA allows each class to have its own unique spread, stretch, and tilt. This mathematical flexibility is what creates curved boundaries.

QDA Pipeline: Labeled data → Split Train/Test → Fit class-specific shapes → Score new test coordinates → Make prediction → Evaluate performance

The Overfitting Trap
BEFORE YOU START

Model selection is part of model fitting. Every candidate comparison must be contained inside the training or cross-validation process.

Building a predictive model is tricky. It is tempting to include every available piece of data. We often assume that more clues guarantee better answers.

However, adding too many variables introduces massive noise. This noise obscures the true relationship. The model ends up memorizing random accidents in the training data rather than learning the actual signal.

The Illusion of Accuracy: A highly complex model performs flawlessly on its "homework" (the training data). But it collapses in the real world on unseen data. This failure is called overfitting.

STAGE 02 · UNDERSTAND
The n-p Puzzle

To build a reliable model, we must balance two things. First is the number of samples (
𝑛
). Second is the number of variables or clues (
𝑝
).

Think of this in three simple steps:

Step 1: You need enough examples to prove a real pattern exists.
Step 2: Every new variable adds a whole new dimension for the model to search.
Step 3: When

>
𝑛
, ordinary least squares has no unique coefficient solution unless constraints are imposed. Ridge, Lasso, or other regularisation can still support useful prediction, although instability and overfitting are serious concerns.

At this point, the design matrix is rank deficient. Without additional constraints, many coefficient vectors may fit the training data equally well. This makes coefficient interpretation unstable and creates a high risk of overfitting. Useful prediction may still be possible with appropriate regularisation, feature structure and honest validation.

Keep the ideas separate: non-unique coefficients concern identifiability; interpolation means matching the observed training outcomes; overfitting is poor generalisation caused by learning sample-specific patterns; predictive performance must be measured on unseen data. Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net impose different constraints that can produce estimable predictors, but they are not automatic cures.

STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
Picking the Best Team

One way to fix this is Subset Selection. This means literally picking a specific group of variables and throwing the rest out.

FORWARD Start empty. Add the single best predictor. Then add the next one that helps the most. Keep going.

BACKWARD Start with all variables. Find the weakest predictor and bench them. Repeat until only the best are left.

HYBRID Add the best predictors one by one. But constantly re-evaluate. If an old predictor becomes redundant, remove it.

It decreases accuracy.
It is computationally impossible. Just 40 predictors creates over a billion models.

The "Super-Variable" Secret

If we have 100 highly correlated variables, they provide redundant information. Dimension Reduction allows us to "squish" them into a few super-variables called Principal Components.

Compress first, predict later. It squishes variables together without looking at what you are trying to predict.

Common Mistakes

Even advanced statistical methods are not magic. Here is how to avoid common traps.

MISTAKE 1

Choosing a model based on training accuracy.

CORRECT PRACTICE

Always compare and judge models based on cross-validation error. Training accuracy is always overly optimistic.

MISTAKE 2

Testing on the final test set multiple times.

CORRECT PRACTICE

Lock the final test set in a vault. Use it only once at the very end to check your final model. If you use it to tweak parameters, it is no longer an honest test.

COMPLETE THE PICTURE
Prefer the simplest near-best model

Validation scores contain noise. The one-standard-error rule chooses the simplest model whose performance is within one standard error of the best observed score.

When comparing many pipelines, use nested cross-validation or a final untouched test set. Otherwise the “best” model may simply be the one that benefited most from repeated checking.

The ultimate goal is Generalization. We want to build a model that stays trustworthy and useful when reality shows up and starts ruining everyone's assumptions.

STAGE 01 · OBSERVE
Points, labels, and a decision boundary

Each point is one labelled training row with two features. Colour marks the class. A classifier needs a rule that places a future point on one side or the other.

f(x) > 0  →  Class +1
f(x) < 0  →  Class −1

In two dimensions the boundary is a line. In three dimensions it is a plane. Beyond that, it becomes a hyperplane, a dramatic name for the same separating idea.

The plot uses two features because humans remain tragically dependent on visible space. The model itself can work with many features.
STAGE 02 · QUESTION
Why not choose any separating line?

When the classes are separable, several lines can classify every training point correctly. Training accuracy alone cannot tell us which line is safer.

Narrow clearance

Fits the training rows, but a small measurement change can flip a prediction.

Wide clearance

Leaves more room before the nearest point crosses the boundary.

A linear SVM adds a preference: choose the separator with the greatest distance to the closest points from either class.

Quick check: what extra criterion does SVM use?
STAGE 03 · UNDERSTAND
The margin is protected space

The margin is the gap between two parallel support planes touching the closest training points on each side.

Boundary: wᵀx + b = 0
Margin boundaries: wᵀx + b = +1 and −1
Geometric margin width = 2 / ‖w‖

Maximising the margin is equivalent to keeping the weight vector small while still satisfying the classification constraints.

A wide margin can make the separator less sensitive. It cannot rescue biased data, leakage, poor labels, or a mismatched kernel. Geometry is useful, not divine intervention.
STAGE 04 · FOCUS
Support vectors are the points that matter most

Support vectors lie on or inside the margin. They directly constrain the fitted boundary.

f(x) = Σᵢ αᵢ yᵢ K(xᵢ, x) + b
Only rows with αᵢ > 0 are support vectors.

Move a distant, safely classified point a little and the boundary may not change. Move a support vector and the solution can shift immediately.

Important distinction: “support vector” means the row constrains this fitted margin. It does not mean the row is causally or commercially important in every possible sense.
STAGE 05 · RELAX
Hard margins break when reality overlaps

A hard-margin SVM demands perfect separation with every row outside the margin. Real classes overlap, labels contain errors, and outliers appear because datasets enjoy sabotage.

A soft-margin SVM introduces slack variables ξᵢ so violations are allowed but penalised.

yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 − ξᵢ,  with ξᵢ ≥ 0
SLACK	MEANING
ξ = 0	Correct and on or beyond the margin
0 < ξ ≤ 1	Correct side, but inside the margin
ξ > 1	Misclassified
STAGE 06 · TUNE
C decides how expensive violations are
minimise  ½‖w‖² + C Σᵢ ξᵢ
Small C

Violations are cheaper. The model accepts more errors to preserve a wider, smoother margin.

Large C

Violations are expensive. The model fits training rows more aggressively, often with a narrower margin.

C is an inverse regularisation parameter: larger C means less regularisation.

A huge C does not mean “more accurate”. It means “punish training violations more”, which can also mean “memorise the noise with confidence”.
STAGE 07 · PREPARE
Scale features before comparing distances

SVM geometry uses dot products and distances. A feature ranging from 0 to 100,000 can dominate another ranging from 0 to 1, even when the smaller-scale feature is genuinely informative.

standardised value = (value − training mean) ÷ training standard deviation

Fit the scaler inside each training fold, then apply that fitted transformation to validation, test, and production rows.

Two distinct failures: scaling before the split leaks information; scaling the test set separately changes the coordinate system. Both are wrong in impressively different ways.
STAGE 08 · FORMALISE
Hinge loss ignores easy correct points
hinge loss = max(0, 1 − y × f(x))
SIGNED MARGIN Y F(X)	LOSS	INTERPRETATION
≥ 1	0	Correct and safely beyond the margin
0 to 1	positive	Correct but inside the margin
≤ 0	≥ 1	Misclassified

Once a point is correctly beyond the margin, its hinge loss is zero. Distant easy points stop pulling the boundary.

STAGE 09 · INTERPRET
The decision score is not automatically a probability

The decision function reports which side of the boundary a row occupies and how strongly it lies in that direction.

larger positive f(x) → stronger Class +1 decision
larger negative f(x) → stronger Class −1 decision

For a linear SVM, the score relates to signed distance after accounting for ‖w‖. For a kernel SVM, treat it as a boundary score rather than literal distance in the original plot.

f(x) = 2 does not mean 200%, nor twice the probability of f(x) = 1. Probability estimates require a separate calibration model fitted with held-out predictions.
STAGE 10 · EXTEND
A straight boundary cannot solve every pattern

Imagine one class forming an inner cluster and another forming an outer ring. No straight line can separate them in the original two-feature space.

A transformed feature such as squared radius can reveal the structure:

r² = x₁² + x₂²

In transformed space, a simple threshold on r² can separate inner from outer points. A curved boundary in the original plot can still correspond to a linear rule elsewhere.

STAGE 11 · KERNELISE
The kernel trick avoids explicit feature explosion

A kernel computes similarities that behave like inner products in a richer feature space, without explicitly constructing every transformed coordinate.

K(x, z) = φ(x)ᵀφ(z)

RBF: K(x,z) = exp(−γ ‖x − z‖²)
Small gamma

Each point has broad influence. The decision surface changes slowly.

Large gamma

Influence becomes local. The boundary can wrap tightly around training points.

Large gamma plus large C can create an intricate boundary that remembers noise instead of learning structure.

STAGE 15 · REFLECT
Reality Check: Limitations

While extremely powerful and explainable, single regression trees have key engineering limitations that you must look out for in practice.

 Poor Extrapolation
Trend Fail

Trees predict flat averages. If a house size is larger than any seen in training (e.g., 220 m²), the tree cannot continue a trend upward; it flatlines at the average of the largest leaf.

 Jagged Step Predictions
Staircase

Real-world factors often rise smoothly. Trees build staircases with sudden step jumps, struggling to cleanly represent smooth curves without huge depths.

 High Instability (Variance)
High Variance

A tiny shift in data (e.g., swapping one point's price) can completely re-arrange the root split boundary, producing a highly unstable prediction layout.

 Axis-Aligned Splits
Orthogonal

Basic trees split one feature at a time at right angles, making it difficult to capture diagonal correlations (like price dropping when size decreases and age increases simultaneously).

 Easy to Overfit
High Complexity

Without strict stopping rules or pruning, deep trees will easily grow until they isolate every single point, memorizing individual training points instead of discovering generalizable patterns.

STAGE 16 · REFLECT
Synthesis

Let's review the final sequence to build and use a regression tree:

1.
Put all training data in the Root Node.
2.
Test possible splits (greedy thresholds) across all available features.
3.
Pick the feature/split that results in the lowest RSS.
4.
Repeat the process recursively inside each new branch.
5.
Use validation error to choose stopping rules or pruning, instead of trusting training error alone.
6.
Each final leaf predicts the average target value inside that leaf.

While a single regression tree can be unstable on its own, this recursive logic is the fundamental building block for advanced modern algorithms like Random Forests and Gradient Boosting.

Ensemble Learning: Ensembles improve single trees by combining hundreds of them, smoothing out jagged steps and yielding highly stable predictions.

Extrapolation and uncertainty

A regression tree cannot naturally extrapolate a trend beyond the training range. New extreme values usually inherit the prediction of the outermost leaf.

Single-tree predictions can be unstable. Ensembles such as random forests or gradient boosting reduce variance, while conformal or bootstrap methods can add uncertainty estimates when required.

Learning is a repeated correction loop. The network guesses, measures how wrong it was, works out which parameters influenced the mistake, and makes a small adjustment.

WHY IT MATTERS

A loss number alone says only “this was wrong.” Backpropagation turns that complaint into useful directions for millions of parameters, allowing each one to change in proportion to its contribution.

Forward propagation moves a batch through the layers and produces predictions.
